lines: You found an apartment for 900 dollars a month. The landlord checks your credit and finds no history, so you pay an extra 900 dollar deposit. Your cousin Ana has a 760 score and pays no extra deposit.

Your credit report is your record of borrowing: every card and loan, and whether you paid on time. Three bureaus keep it: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You can see all three free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com.
Your FICO score runs from 300 to 850. 670 and up is good, 740 is very good, and 800 is exceptional. The U.S. average is about 715.
Five things move it. Payment history counts 35 percent. Amounts owed, 30. Length of history, 15. New credit and credit mix, 10 each.
Utilization is your card balance divided by your limit. 40 dollars on a 500 dollar limit is 8 percent. Keep it under 30 percent, and under 10 is best.
A payment 30 or more days late stays on your report for 7 years. Applying for credit is a hard inquiry. Checking your own score is a soft inquiry and never hurts it.
Your income, your savings and your debit card are not part of your score.
To start from zero, open a secured card, put one small bill on it, and pay it in full with autopay. After about 6 months, you'll have a score.
On a 20,000 dollar car loan, a lower score can cost about 3,500 dollars more. Like reef fish choosing the cleaner with the good record, lenders check yours first.
